# Derivation of the Exponential Energy Factor {#appendix-energy}

In Lecture \@ref(lecture5), we used the result that the fraction of collisions with enough energy to react, i.e., with head-on collision energy greater than or equal to the activation energy $E_\mathrm{a}$, is given by:

$$P(E \geq E_\mathrm{a}) = \exp\left(-\frac{E_\mathrm{a}}{RT}\right)$$

This expression can be derived from the kinetic theory of gases.

### Head-On Collision Energy

Consider a molecule B approaching a molecule A. We can split the velocity of B relative to A into two parts: a component $v$ along the line joining the centres of the two molecules when they collide, and a component perpendicular to this line. Only the component along the line of centres pushes the molecules together; the perpendicular component carries them past each other. The head-on collision energy is the kinetic energy associated with the component along the line of centres:

$$E = \frac{1}{2}\mu v^2$$

where $\mu$ is the reduced mass of A and B.

### The Distribution of Head-On Velocities

The kinetic theory of gases tells us that each component of the relative velocity of a pair of molecules follows a Gaussian (Maxwell-Boltzmann) distribution:

$$g(v) = \left(\frac{\mu}{2\pi k_\mathrm{B}T}\right)^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\mu v^2}{2k_\mathrm{B}T}\right)$$

where $k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature. Because a gas has no preferred direction, this holds whichever direction the line of centres points in.

The distribution $g(v)$ describes pairs of molecules, but the pairs that collide in a given time are not a random sample of all pairs. A pair approaching quickly closes the gap between the two molecules sooner than a pair approaching slowly, so the rate at which pairs with approach velocity $v$ collide is proportional to $v$ as well as to $g(v)$. Only pairs that are approaching each other collide, so $v > 0$. The distribution of head-on velocities across all collisions is therefore

$$h(v) \propto v\exp\left(-\frac{\mu v^2}{2k_\mathrm{B}T}\right) \qquad (v > 0)$$

### From Velocities to Energies

To convert this into a distribution of head-on collision energies, we change variables from $v$ to $E = \frac{1}{2}\mu v^2$, so that $\mathrm{d}E = \mu v\,\mathrm{d}v$. The factor of $v$ in $h(v)$ then cancels:

$$h(v)\,\mathrm{d}v \propto v\exp\left(-\frac{E}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right)\frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mu v} \propto \exp\left(-\frac{E}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right)\mathrm{d}E$$

The head-on collision energies therefore follow a simple exponential distribution. Normalising, so that $\int_0^{\infty} p(E)\,\mathrm{d}E = 1$, gives

$$p(E) = \frac{1}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\exp\left(-\frac{E}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right)$$

which is the distribution plotted in Figure \@ref(fig:fig-maxwell-boltzmann).

### Calculating the Fraction with E ≥ E_a

The fraction of collisions with head-on energy greater than or equal to $E_\mathrm{a}$ is obtained by integrating this distribution from $E_\mathrm{a}$ to infinity:

$$P(E \geq E_\mathrm{a}) = \int_{E_\mathrm{a}}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\exp\left(-\frac{E}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right)\mathrm{d}E = \exp\left(-\frac{E_\mathrm{a}}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right)$$

Finally, using the relationship $R = N_\mathrm{A}k_\mathrm{B}$ (where $R$ is the gas constant and $N_\mathrm{A}$ is Avogadro's number), we can write this in the more familiar form, with $E_\mathrm{a}$ now a molar energy:

$$P(E \geq E_\mathrm{a}) = \exp\left(-\frac{E_\mathrm{a}}{RT}\right)$$

This derivation shows that the exponential dependence of reaction rates on temperature arises naturally from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular speeds, and that the activation energy $E_\mathrm{a}$ represents a threshold that determines which fraction of collisions have sufficient energy to react.
